I've organised the notes verse by verse below. Each point gives its source URL. Some points come from pages I read in full (Enduring Word, Wesley's Notes and the Haydock Catholic commentary on Bible Hub), so they carry a URL but no inline citation.

**What I couldn't find:** nothing from the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), any Orthodox page (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org directly, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on verses 1–23. The only NET Bible point comes second-hand through bible.org. I also found little that deals specifically with verses 10–12 or 16–17.

## Matthew 25:1–13: The ten virgins

**v. 1**
- **Wedding customs (Guzik):** A Jewish wedding then had three stages: engagement, betrothal, and the marriage itself about a year later. Guzik cites a report that Talmudic authorities said a bridal procession usually had ten lamps. He quotes Carson that the point is the number of girls invited, not their virginity. He follows France in taking the bridegroom as Jesus, which France calls a bold image because the Old Testament usually calls *God* Israel's bridegroom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Who the virgins stand for. This is a real split.**
  - **Reformed/Anglican (Ryle):** The professing Church is compared to "ten virgins, who took their lamps, and went out to meet the bridegroom." https://www.monergism.com/parable-ten-virgins
  - **Dispensational (Got Questions):** It rejects a rapture reading and takes the parable as Christ's second coming at the end of the tribulation, holding that all the parables in this series relate to Israel, not the church. https://www.gotquestions.org/parable-ten-virgins.html
  - **Dispensational (Thomas Ice):** Ice agrees: the ten stand for Israel as a nation, and the two groups are believing and prepared Israel and unbelieving Israel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/ice_thomas/Mat24-25/Mat24-25_Part37.cfm
  - **Methodist (Wesley):** The "kingdom of heaven" here means the people hoping to enter it, whom Wesley calls the candidates for it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The ten stand for all humanity, the bridegroom for Christ, the bride for the Church, and the oil for grace and charity. Haydock also cites Gregory, who saw the Church on earth as a mix of good and bad, like wise and foolish virgins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

**v. 2**
- **Guzik:** He quotes Bruce that the contrast is not "bad and good" but prudent and thoughtless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Barnes:** He warns against reading the five-and-five split as a statistic. There is no authority for saying that he meant to teach that just half of professing Christians would be deceived. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/25-4.htm
- **Church Fathers (in Aquinas's Catena Aurea):** Hilary takes the two groups as an absolute distinction between believers and unbelievers. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxv.html

**v. 3**
- **The lamps:** Following France, Guzik says these were probably torches, oil-soaked rags wrapped on a stick, not standing lamps. The foolish *looked* ready because they held lamps, but they had brought no oil. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Did the foolish ever have oil? Commentators disagree.**
  - **Deffinbaugh (bible.org):** He notes that a footnote in the NET Bible indicates that the word "extra" is not found in the Greek text. He argues the foolish never had oil at all: These five foolish virgins were not once saved, but then "ran out" of salvation. They were lost, and never had it. https://bible.org/seriespage/ten-virgins-what-it-means-be-ready-matthew-251-13
  - **Matthew Henry:** They had just the oil enough to make their lamps burn for the present, to make a show with. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_025.cfm
  - **Wesley:** The lamp is faith. A lamp and oil with it, is faith working by love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm

**v. 4: What the oil means. The clearest split between traditions.**
- **Holy Spirit (Guzik):** Oil is often a picture of the Holy Spirit, and without the Holy Spirit, no one is ready for the return of Jesus. He thinks Jesus was probably separating true Christians from false believers, not "Spirit-filled" from other Christians. He still urges readers to keep being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Holy Spirit (Ryle):** Let us never rest until we know that we have the oil of the Spirit in our hearts. https://www.monergism.com/parable-ten-virgins
- **Holy Spirit, or possibly faith (Got Questions):** Olive oil can also be seen as a symbol of the Holy Spirit (or possibly of faith). https://www.gotquestions.org/olive-oil-symbol.html
- **Reformed (Gill):** The oil is grace, given freely and not gained by free will. Gill writes that it was freely given unto them, and powerfully wrought in them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/25-4.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Grace is the oil which we must have in this vessel. https://www.monergism.com/parable-ten-virgins-0
- **Methodist (Wesley):** The oil is love in their hearts. And they daily sought a fresh supply of spiritual strength, till their faith was made perfect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The oil is grace and charity joined to faith. The extra supply in the flasks is a store of good works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm
- **Church Fathers (Catena Aurea):** They give several meanings:
  - Hilary: The "oil" is the fruit of good works.
  - Augustine: the oil is joy.
  - Chrysostom: charity, alms, and every aid rendered to the needy.
  - https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxv.html
- **Chrysostom's own homily:** He takes the lamps as virginity and by oil, humanity, almsgiving, succor to them that are in need. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200178.htm

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:** Both the wise and the foolish slept. The difference was that the wise were ready to act the moment they woke. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Piper (Baptist):** All ten slept, not just the foolish, which means that sleep in this parable is not negative. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/the-end-is-near-are-you-ready
- **Matthew Henry** is more critical: The wise virgins kept their lamps burning, but did not keep themselves awake. https://www.monergism.com/parable-ten-virgins-0
- **Wesley:** All slept peacefully, the wise with a true peace and the foolish with a false one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Catholic (Haydock):** Following Jerome, sleeping here means dying. It is called "slumber" because they will rise again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm
- **Against the partial-rapture view:** Some teach that only watchful Christians will be taken in the rapture. Ice answers that if watchfulness is necessary for worthiness, as partial rapturists characteristically argue, then none of the ten virgins qualify. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/ice_thomas/Mat24-25/Mat24-25_Part37.cfm

**v. 6**
- **Wesley:** Midnight means in an hour quite unthought of. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Haydock:** Following Augustine, the cry stands for the last trumpet and the general resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm
- **Chrysostom:** He links the cry to Paul's "shout… voice of an archangel" (1 Thessalonians 4:16). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200178.htm

**v. 7**
- **Guzik:** "Trimmed" literally means "put their torches in order." He quotes France that until this crisis there was no visible difference between the two groups. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Wesley:** Trimming the lamps means They examined themselves and prepared to meet their God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm

**v. 8**
- **Wesley:** "Our lamps are going out" means Our faith is dead. What a time to discover this! https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It argues the foolish had something at first. The lamps of the foolish virgins once had light, else they could not have "gone out." Elsewhere it warns against put[ting] our trust in the grace once given in holy baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/matthew-25.html
- **Can believers fall away? Protestant traditions disagree here.**
  - **Coffman (Restoration Movement, Arminian):** The foolish virgins are the Lord's own example of saved persons who at last failed to make the port of everlasting life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/25-1.html
  - **Deffinbaugh (bible.org)** takes the opposite view: they were never saved (see v. 3).
- **Gregory (Catena Aurea):** The lamps go out because works that looked bright to people turn out empty when the Judge comes. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxv.html

**v. 9**
- **Faith can't be borrowed (Barclay):** A man cannot borrow a relationship with God; he must possess it for himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/25-1.html
- **Wesley:** "Those who sell" means God, or Christ, who sells "without money and without price." But the time to buy is past. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Protestant vs. Catholic:** Matthew Henry uses this verse against Rome: The church of Rome, which dreams of works of supererogation and the imputation of the righteousness of saints, forgets that it was the wisdom of the wise virgins to understand that they had but oil enough for themselves. (Supererogation means good works beyond what God requires, which Catholic teaching says can benefit others.) https://www.monergism.com/parable-ten-virgins-0
- **Catholic and patristic readings of "those who sell":**
  - Hilary: They that sell are the poor, who give back the merit of good works in return for alms.
  - Augustine offers another option: the sellers are flatterers, and the line is an ironic rebuke.
  - https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxv.html
  - Haydock follows Augustine's reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

**v. 10**
- **Matthew Henry:** Getting grace is a work of time, and cannot be done in a hurry. https://www.monergism.com/parable-ten-virgins-0
- **Haydock:** Jerome says no prayers or good works will count after the final judgment. Augustine says the gate of heaven is then closed for ever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm
- **Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik):** Once shut, the door never opens again. He rejects any hope of a second chance after death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/

**vv. 11–12**
- **Guzik:** He quotes France that "I do not know you" echoes Matthew 7:22–23 and is a formal rejection, not just a statement of fact. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Jerome (Catena Aurea):** "The Lord knoweth them that are his," so those without oil are unknown, even if they are pure in body or correct in their confession of faith. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxv.html

**v. 13**
- **Guzik:** The point is simple: be ready. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Wesley:** He that watches has not only a burning lamp, but likewise oil in his vessel. And even when he sleepeth, his heart waketh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Ice:** In his view "watch" here means being genuinely regenerated and indwelt by the Spirit rather than having unusual spirituality. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/ice_thomas/Mat24-25/Mat24-25_Part37.cfm
- **Augustine (via Haydock):** We cannot stay awake all the time. We "watch" with the heart through faith, hope, charity and good works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

## Matthew 25:14–23: The talents

**v. 14**
- **Guzik:** Leaving property with trusted servants was normal and sensible in the ancient world. He quotes France: this parable answers what "readiness" actually *is*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Wesley:** The "kingdom of heaven" here means its King, Christ. He reads the parable as a warning about the fate of a merely "harmless" man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Haydock:** Following Gregory, the man is Christ, who went "into a far country" when he ascended in his human nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

**v. 15: What are the talents?**
- **Money, applied to life resources (Guzik):** A talent was a sum of money, not an ability. It is fair to apply it to time, money, abilities and authority. Carson reckons one talent was about twenty years of a labourer's wages. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Deffinbaugh (bible.org):** The talents were distributed on the basis of ability, not as the bestowing of ability. https://bible.org/seriespage/27-parable-talents-matthew-2514-30-luke-1912-28
- **Gifts and abilities (desiringgod.org):** It reads the parable as being about stewarding the gifts and abilities God entrusts to us. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/have-you-buried-your-gifts
- **All God has entrusted (Constable):** Probably we should understand the talents to represent all the working capital that God entrusts to His disciples. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/25-15.html
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Christ does not distinguish between natural gifts and the gifts of the Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/25-15.html
- **Reformed (Gill):** The talents cannot mean saving grace. That grace can never be lost, yet one servant loses his talent and is cast out. So Gill takes the talents as outward gifts, especially gifts for ministry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/25-15.htm
- **Methodist (Wesley):** "According to his ability" may be translated more literally, according to his own mighty power. He also says the master's journey was "to heaven." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/25-15.html
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** *Five* talents would be *too much* for some men: *one* talent would be *too little*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/25-15.html
- **Catholic (Haydock):** We can do no good by ourselves, only by God's grace, but God requires our cooperation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- **Guzik:** "Went at once" shows they took the job seriously and started without delay. We aren't told how they traded. Their work was prompt, persevering and successful. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Matthew Henry:** He applies "trading" to using the Bible, the sacraments and the gifts of the Spirit: this is trading with our talents. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/25-15.html

**v. 18**
- **Guzik:** The third servant made sure the money wasn't lost, but he did nothing positive with it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Wesley:** He used having fewer talents than the others as an excuse to improve none. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/25.htm
- **Gregory (via Haydock):** Burying the talent means using God's gifts only for earthly things. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

**v. 19**
- **Guzik:** The long delay tempted the servants to think they would never be called to account. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Jerome (via Haydock):** The delay is the time between Christ's ascension and his return. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

**v. 20**
- **Catholic (Haydock):** Haydock says this verse shows that free will, helped by God's grace, truly merits reward. Protestant sources would dispute this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

**v. 21**
- **Faithfulness, not brilliance (Guzik):** The master looked first for goodness and faithfulness, not a set profit. Guzik quotes Spurgeon that the praise is not "Well done, good and brilliant servant." He says "the joy of your master" points to heaven, and quotes Spurgeon that this is the master's own joy shared with his servants. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/

**vv. 22–23**
- **The same reward for both (Guzik):** Both servants got the same reward even though they started with different amounts. Each did equally well with what he had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-25/
- **Matthew Henry:** Our comfort, in the day of account, will be according to our faithfulness, not according to our usefulness; our sincerity, not our success. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/25-15.html
- **The Gospel Coalition:** It points out that the two servants get word-for-word the same praise. Its lesson: Faithfulness matters more than results. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/less-talent/
- **Catholic (Haydock):** Following Jansenius, the equal reward shows God judges by what each person received. However humble someone's gifts, they can enter heaven as easily as the most learned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/matthew/25.htm

---

**Main differences in brief:**
- **What the oil means:** the Holy Spirit (Guzik, Ryle, Pulpit), grace (Henry, Gill), love working with faith (Wesley), or charity, good works and almsgiving (Catholic writers and Chrysostom).
- **Whether the foolish ever had real faith:** never saved (Deffinbaugh, Gill), versus saved people who were finally lost (Coffman).
- **Who the virgins are:** the church (Ryle, Henry) or Israel at the end of the age (Got Questions, Ice).
- **Merit (vv. 9 and 20):** Catholic teaching on merit and on the good works of saints helping others (Haydock) versus Henry's Protestant rejection of it.
